stills.heading: Melodic and Harmonic Motion
stills.caption: Lesson 7 · Harmony Course · Storm Studios Learning
stills.narration: Hello, and welcome back to Storm Studios Learning. In the previous lesson we learned how to build chords for the vocal quartet. Today we are going to see how the voices move when we go from one chord to the next.

stills.heading: Two parts
stills.caption: Melodic motion · harmonic motion
stills.narration: This lesson has two parts: melodic motion and harmonic motion.

stills.heading: Melodic motion
stills.caption: A single voice, from one note to the next
stills.narration: Melodic motion is about a single voice, and the intervals it sings from one note to the next.

stills.heading: Harmonic motion
stills.caption: Two voices moving at the same time
stills.narration: Harmonic motion is about two voices moving at the same time.

stills.heading: Each voice sings its own melody
stills.caption: Before the first chorale, we practice each voice on its own
stills.narration: When we connect two chords, each voice sings its own melody. That is why, before we write our first chorale, we are going to practice each voice on its own.

stills.heading: Step by step
stills.caption: First each voice, then connections, then the chorale
stills.narration: I remember my first chorale very well. There are so many things to watch at the same time that it is very easy to get lost. So let's go step by step.

stills.heading: Melodic motion
stills.narration: Let's start with melodic motion.

stills.heading: Allowed intervals
stills.narration: When one chord connects to another, each voice can only use these intervals.

stills.heading: Minor second and major second
stills.narration: The minor second and the major second.

stills.heading: Minor third and major third
stills.narration: The minor third and the major third.

stills.heading: Perfect fourth and perfect fifth
stills.narration: The perfect fourth and the perfect fifth.

stills.heading: Minor sixth and major sixth
stills.narration: The minor sixth and the major sixth.

stills.heading: Perfect octave
stills.narration: And the perfect octave.

stills.heading: No augmented intervals
stills.caption: No sevenths · nothing larger than an octave
stills.narration: There are no augmented intervals in this list. There are no sevenths either, and nothing larger than an octave.

stills.heading: Four groups
stills.narration: These intervals are classified into four groups.

stills.heading: Step
stills.caption: Seconds
stills.narration: Seconds are called steps.

stills.heading: Short path
stills.caption: Thirds
stills.narration: Thirds are called short paths.

stills.heading: Short leap
stills.caption: The perfect fourth
stills.narration: The perfect fourth is a short leap.

stills.heading: Long leaps
stills.caption: Perfect fifth, sixths and octave
stills.narration: And the perfect fifth, the sixths and the octave are long leaps.

stills.heading: The nine intervals
stills.narration: Let's listen to each one.

stills.heading: The step is the most natural
stills.caption: Leaps give character, with care
stills.narration: The step is the most natural motion for a voice. Leaps give the melody character, but they have to be used with care.

stills.heading: The leading tone: B
stills.caption: It wants to rise to C
stills.narration: The first rule of care has to do with the leading tone. In C major, the leading tone is B, the note that wants to rise to C.

stills.heading: No octave leaps on the leading tone
stills.narration: The leading tone never leaps an octave.

stills.heading: Diminished intervals
stills.narration: Now let's look at diminished intervals. We said that augmented intervals are not used.

stills.heading: Diminished 5th, 4th and 7th
stills.caption: Allowed if the voice then changes direction: compensating
stills.narration: But the diminished fifth, the diminished fourth and the diminished seventh are allowed, on one condition. After the diminished interval, the voice has to change direction. We call this compensating.

stills.heading: B – F upward
stills.caption: Diminished fifth
stills.narration: In C major, from B up to F there is a diminished fifth.

stills.heading: Compensated
stills.caption: The voice moves down
stills.narration: If the voice then moves down, for example to E, the diminished fifth is compensated.

stills.heading: F – B downward
stills.caption: Also a diminished fifth
stills.narration: From F down to B there is also a diminished fifth.

stills.heading: Compensated
stills.caption: The voice moves up
stills.narration: If the voice then moves up, for example to C, it is also compensated.

stills.heading: Not compensated
stills.caption: After B and F it goes on to G
stills.narration: But if after B and F the voice keeps rising, to G, the diminished fifth is left uncompensated.

stills.heading: F – B upward: augmented fourth
stills.caption: Augmented fourths are not used
stills.narration: And watch the direction. From F up to B there is no diminished fifth, but an augmented fourth. And augmented fourths are not used.

stills.heading: Diminished 4th and 7th
stills.caption: They appear in the minor mode · we will see them later
stills.narration: The diminished fourth and the diminished seventh appear in the minor mode, and we will see them later.

stills.heading: Successive leaps
stills.caption: Same direction: only a 4th and a 5th, or a 5th and a 4th
stills.narration: The last melodic rule is about successive leaps. Two leaps in a row in the same direction are not used. The exception is a fourth followed by a fifth, or a fifth followed by a fourth.

stills.heading: C – F – C
stills.narration: For example, from C to F and then to C, going up, is fine.

stills.heading: C – G – C
stills.narration: From C to G and then to C, too.

stills.heading: D – G – C
stills.caption: Two fourths upward
stills.narration: But from D to G and then to C are two fourths going up, and that is not used.

stills.heading: Change of direction
stills.caption: No problem
stills.narration: If the voice changes direction after a leap, there is no problem.

stills.heading: Harmonic motion
stills.caption: Two voices moving at the same time
stills.narration: Now let's move on to harmonic motion. Here we no longer look at a single voice, but at two voices moving at the same time.

stills.heading: Parallel fifths and octaves
stills.caption: The most famous rule in harmony
stills.narration: The first rule is the most famous one in all of harmony. Parallel fifths and parallel octaves are not used. There are parallel fifths or octaves when two voices form a fifth or an octave, and then, moving in the same direction, form a fifth or an octave again.

stills.heading: Parallel octaves
stills.caption: Soprano C5 – D5 · bass C3 – D3
stills.narration: For example, the soprano goes from C five to D five, and the bass goes from C three to D three. The two voices are an octave apart, and they stay an octave apart.

stills.heading: Parallel octaves
stills.narration: Let's listen.

stills.heading: They sound like a single voice
stills.caption: We lose a voice of the quartet
stills.narration: With parallel octaves, the two voices sound as if they were only one. We lose a voice of the quartet.

stills.heading: Parallel fifths
stills.caption: The voices blend and the sound becomes hollow
stills.narration: Something similar happens with parallel fifths. The perfect fifth is such a stable interval that the two voices blend and the sound becomes hollow.

stills.heading: Contrary fifths and octaves
stills.caption: The same, in opposite directions
stills.narration: Contrary fifths and contrary octaves are not used either. They are the same fifths or octaves, but with the voices moving in opposite directions.

stills.heading: Contrary octaves
stills.caption: Soprano G4 – C5 · bass G3 – C3
stills.narration: For example, the soprano rises from G four to C five while the bass falls from G three to C three. We go from one octave to two octaves, and the effect is the same.

stills.heading: The unison counts as an octave
stills.narration: The unison also counts as an octave.

stills.heading: Allowed fifths
stills.caption: Two cases
stills.narration: Now, there are two cases in which fifths are allowed.

stills.heading: Parallel fifths that are not perfect
stills.narration: The first is parallel fifths when one of the two, or both, are not perfect.

stills.heading: Perfect → diminished
stills.narration: For example, from a perfect fifth to a diminished fifth.

stills.heading: Diminished → perfect
stills.narration: Or from a diminished fifth to a perfect fifth.

stills.heading: Perfect → perfect: no
stills.narration: What is not allowed is going from one perfect fifth to another perfect fifth.

stills.heading: Outer voices
stills.caption: The soprano and the bass: the top one and the bottom one
stills.narration: The second case is contrary fifths in voices that are not the outer voices. The outer voices are the soprano and the bass, the top one and the bottom one.

stills.heading: Soprano and bass: no
stills.narration: Between the soprano and the bass, contrary fifths are not used.

stills.heading: Tenor and bass: yes
stills.narration: But between the tenor and the bass, for example, they are allowed.

stills.heading: Simultaneous leaps
stills.narration: The last harmonic rule is about simultaneous leaps.

stills.heading: Two leaps in the same direction
stills.narration: We avoid two voices leaping at the same time in the same direction.

stills.heading: Exception: two perfect fourths
stills.narration: The exception is when both leaps are perfect fourths.

stills.heading: Opposite directions
stills.caption: No problem
stills.narration: If two voices leap at the same time but in opposite directions, there is no problem.

stills.heading: IV – V with parallel fifths
stills.caption: Tenor and bass
stills.narration: Let's listen to a connection of two chords with parallel fifths.

stills.heading: IV – V written correctly
stills.narration: And now the same connection, written correctly.

stills.heading: Coming lessons
stills.caption: Harmonic material and connections · two-chord connections · first chorale
stills.narration: We will practice the harmonic rules when we start connecting chords. First we will see which chords we can use and how they connect. Then you will write connections of two chords. And after that you will write your first complete chorale.

stills.heading: Assignment for the Virtual Teacher
stills.narration: Now, the assignment for the Virtual Teacher.

stills.heading: Four exercises
stills.caption: Soprano · alto · tenor · bass · each one uploaded separately
stills.narration: This time there are four exercises, one for each voice: soprano, alto, tenor and bass. Each exercise is uploaded separately.

stills.heading: Eight quarter notes, two measures
stills.caption: Any major key · begins and ends on the tonic
stills.narration: In each one you will write a melody of eight notes, in quarter notes, that is, two measures of four four. You can choose any major key, and it can be different in each exercise. The melody begins and ends on the first degree, the tonic.

stills.heading: SATB Quartet mode
stills.caption: Only the staff of the voice you are practicing
stills.narration: Work in the sequencer in SATB Quartet mode. Write the melody only on the staff of the voice you are practicing, and leave the others empty. That way the Virtual Teacher knows which voice it is.

stills.heading: Allowed intervals
stills.caption: Melodic motion rules · no repeated notes
stills.narration: Use only the allowed intervals and follow the rules of melodic motion. In this exercise notes are not repeated. When we connect chords we will be able to repeat them, but for now every note moves to a different one.

stills.heading: Within the range of each voice
stills.narration: And stay within the range of each voice.

stills.heading: Soprano
stills.caption: C4 to G5
stills.narration: The soprano, from C four to G five.

stills.heading: Alto
stills.caption: G3 to D5
stills.narration: The alto, from G three to D five.

stills.heading: Tenor
stills.caption: B2 to G4
stills.narration: The tenor, from B two to G four.

stills.heading: Bass
stills.caption: F2 to B3
stills.narration: And the bass, from F two to B three.

stills.heading: Export each melody as MIDI
stills.caption: And upload it to the Virtual Teacher
stills.narration: Export each melody as a MIDI file and upload it.

stills.heading: The Virtual Teacher checks
stills.caption: Voice and key · every interval · range · opening and closing tonic
stills.narration: The Virtual Teacher recognizes the voice and the key. It checks every interval, the range, and that you begin and end on the tonic. And if it finds an error, it tells you what it is and on which notes.

stills.heading: Let's recap
stills.narration: Let's recap.

stills.heading: Allowed intervals
stills.narration: Each voice moves by steps, short paths, short leaps and long leaps. We do not use augmented intervals, sevenths, or intervals larger than an octave.

stills.heading: Diminished: compensated
stills.narration: Diminished intervals are compensated by changing direction.

stills.heading: Leading tone and successive leaps
stills.narration: We do not leap an octave with the leading tone, or make two leaps in a row in the same direction, except a fourth and a fifth.

stills.heading: Between two voices
stills.narration: Between two voices, we avoid parallel and contrary fifths and octaves, and simultaneous leaps in the same direction.

stills.heading: Thank you
stills.caption: See you in lesson 8
stills.narration: Thank you for joining me. See you in lesson eight.
